topics.title: Stone Age to Iron Age
topics.intro: Long before the Romans, people in Britain hunted with stone tools, built Stonehenge, and later learned to make bronze and iron.
topics.teach: Explain the order of the Stone Age, Bronze Age and Iron Age, and why they have those names.
topics.talk: Ask {him} what {she} would have eaten as a Stone Age hunter.

topics.title: Ancient Egypt
topics.intro: Ancient Egypt grew up beside the River Nile more than 4,000 years ago. Its kings, called pharaohs, built enormous pyramids.
topics.teach: Explain why the River Nile was so important to the Egyptians.
topics.talk: Write {her} name in hieroglyphs together (you can find an alphabet online or in a library book).

topics.title: Cars and speed through time
topics.intro: Before cars, people travelled by horse. The first petrol car was built in 1885. Since then, cars have got faster and faster, and one has even broken the sound barrier!
topics.teach: Explain how travel changed from horses to cars.
topics.talk: Ask a grandparent what their first car was like.

topics.title: Great inventors
topics.intro: Inventors are people who come up with new ideas that change the world: telephones, television, the World Wide Web…
topics.teach: Explain which invention you think changed the world the most, and why.
topics.talk: Ask {him} to invent something to solve a problem at home, and draw it.

topics.title: Brave rescues at sea
topics.intro: Britain is surrounded by sea. Lifeboat crews, and one very brave young woman, have risked their lives to rescue sailors in storms.
topics.teach: Explain why Grace Darling became famous.
topics.talk: If you visit the coast, look for the lifeboat station.

topics.title: Explorers
topics.intro: Explorers travel to places no one from their country has been before: across oceans, to the frozen South Pole and to the top of the world’s highest mountain.
topics.teach: Explain why exploring Antarctica was so dangerous.
topics.talk: Ask {him} where in the world {she} would most like to explore.

topics.title: The Victorians
topics.intro: Queen Victoria reigned from 1837 to 1901. It was a time of steam trains, factories, big inventions, and very strict schools!
topics.teach: Explain how a Victorian school was different from yours.
topics.talk: Look for a Victorian building near you: a station, a school or a post box with “VR” on it.

topics.title: The Tudors
topics.intro: The Tudors ruled England from 1485 to 1603. Their kings and queens included Henry VIII and Elizabeth I. It was a time of great ships, explorers and plays.
topics.teach: Explain what happened to the Mary Rose.
topics.talk: Ask {him} why the Tudor rose is red and white.

items.prompt: Put these ages in order, earliest first.
items.explain: Stone tools came first, then bronze (copper mixed with tin), then iron, which is harder still.

items.prompt: Stone Age people made sharp tools from a hard stone called…
items.explain: Flint can be chipped to make a very sharp edge.

items.prompt: Which famous circle of giant stones was built in Britain about 5,000 years ago?
items.explain: Stonehenge is in Wiltshire. Some stones came all the way from Wales!

items.prompt: Which huge hairy elephant did early Stone Age people hunt?
items.explain: Woolly mammoths lived in cold places and had long curved tusks. Dinosaurs were long gone by then.

items.prompt: Skara Brae in Orkney is a Stone Age village. What were its houses built from?
items.explain: Even the beds and cupboards were made of stone, so we can still see them today.

items.prompt: What big change happened when Stone Age people learned to farm?

options.text: They could stay in one place

options.feedback: Farming gave them MORE food.
Tractors came thousands of years later!

items.explain: Growing crops and keeping animals meant people could build villages.

items.prompt: What kind of house did Iron Age families live in?
items.explain: Roundhouses had walls of woven sticks and mud, a thatched roof and a fire in the middle.

items.prompt: Iron Age people built villages on hilltops surrounded by ditches. What are these called?
items.explain: Maiden Castle in Dorset is one of the biggest hill forts.

items.prompt: Which river did the ancient Egyptians live beside?
items.explain: Every year the Nile flooded, leaving rich mud for growing crops.

items.prompt: What were the kings of ancient Egypt called?
items.explain: The pharaoh was thought to be part god.

items.prompt: What were the great pyramids built for?
items.explain: The Great Pyramid of Giza was built about 4,500 years ago for the pharaoh Khufu.

items.prompt: Egyptians preserved dead bodies by drying them and wrapping them in bandages. What do we call these?
items.explain: They believed the body was needed in the afterlife.

items.prompt: What was ancient Egyptian picture writing called?
items.explain: Hieroglyphs used little pictures for sounds and words.

items.prompt: Which boy pharaoh’s tomb, full of gold treasure, was found by Howard Carter in 1922?
items.explain: Tutankhamun became pharaoh when he was about 9 years old.

items.prompt: How did experts learn to read hieroglyphs again?

options.text: The Rosetta Stone also had Greek on it
An old Egyptian taught them how
options.feedback: Nobody had read hieroglyphs for over a thousand years.

options.text: They guessed what each picture meant
options.feedback: They used the Rosetta Stone to compare the writing.

items.explain: Because they could read the Greek, they could work out the hieroglyphs. The stone is in the British Museum.

items.prompt: Which came first: the pyramids of Egypt, or the Romans arriving in Britain?

options.feedback: The Great Pyramid was built around 2560 BC; the Romans invaded in AD 43.

options.text: They happened at the same time
options.feedback: Over 2,500 years apart!

items.explain: The Great Pyramid is about 4,500 years old. Roman Britain began about 2,000 years ago.

items.prompt: Before cars, how did most people travel long distances on land?

options.feedback: Aeroplanes came after cars.

options.text: By rocket or by jet pack
options.feedback: Rockets are much more recent!

items.explain: Horses pulled carriages and carts. Steam trains arrived in the 1800s.

items.prompt: Who built the first petrol car, in 1885?
items.explain: His Motorwagen had three wheels. His wife Bertha drove it on the first long car journey.

items.prompt: In early motoring in Britain, a law said someone had to walk in front of a steam car carrying what?

options.feedback: It was a red flag.
It was a red flag to warn horses and people.

items.explain: The “Red Flag Act” kept speeds very slow. It was scrapped in 1896.

items.prompt: Henry Ford made cars cheaper by building them on a moving line in a factory. Which famous car was it?
items.explain: Ford’s assembly line made millions of Model Ts, so many more people could own a car.

items.prompt: The very first Formula One World Championship race was held in 1950 in which country?
items.explain: It was at Silverstone, a racetrack in Northamptonshire built on an old wartime airfield.

items.prompt: In 1997, a British jet car became the first car to go faster than the speed of sound. What was it called?
items.explain: Driven by Andy Green, it reached 763 miles per hour in a desert in the USA.

items.prompt: Sir Malcolm Campbell broke speed records in cars (and boats) with which name?
items.explain: His son Donald Campbell broke records in Bluebirds too.

items.prompt: How are many new cars today different from old ones?

options.text: They have no wheels at all
options.feedback: They still have wheels!
That was before cars.

items.explain: Electric cars are quieter and make less pollution where they drive.

items.prompt: Who invented the telephone, in 1876?
items.explain: Bell was born in Edinburgh, Scotland.

items.prompt: Which Scottish inventor showed the first working television in 1926?
items.explain: His first pictures were blurry, but they moved!

items.prompt: Which British scientist invented the World Wide Web in 1989?
items.explain: He gave it away for free so everyone could use it.

items.prompt: Which engineer with a tall top hat built bridges, tunnels, a railway and giant steamships?
items.explain: Brunel designed the Clifton Suspension Bridge in Bristol and built the Great Western Railway.

items.prompt: Who wrote what many call the first computer program, in the 1840s?
items.explain: She wrote instructions for a calculating machine that had not even been built yet.

items.prompt: Thomas Edison is famous for making which invention work well enough to use in homes?
items.explain: Edison tested thousands of materials before he found one that worked.

items.prompt: What do all good inventors do?

options.feedback: Edison failed thousands of times before his bulb worked!
Inventors come up with new ideas.

items.explain: Edison is often quoted as saying: “I have not failed. I’ve just found 10,000 ways that won’t work.”

items.prompt: In 1838, which young woman rowed out through a storm with her father to rescue shipwrecked sailors?
items.explain: Grace lived in a lighthouse on the Farne Islands, off the coast of Northumberland.

items.prompt: Where did Grace Darling live?
items.explain: Her father was the lighthouse keeper at Longstone.

items.prompt: Which charity, started in 1824, runs lifeboats around the UK’s coasts?
items.explain: The Royal National Lifeboat Institution. Most of its crews are volunteers.

items.prompt: Most RNLI lifeboat crew are volunteers. What does that mean?

options.text: They are soldiers in the navy
options.feedback: They are ordinary people who give their time.
They are on call day and night.

items.explain: When the pager goes, they leave work or home and race to the lifeboat.

items.prompt: Why was Grace Darling’s rescue so brave?

options.text: The sea was stormy and dangerous

options.feedback: The danger was the storm.

options.text: It was a calm and sunny day
options.feedback: It was a terrible storm!

items.explain: She and her father rowed a small boat over a mile through huge waves.

items.prompt: In an emergency at the seaside, what number do you call and ask for the Coastguard?
items.explain: Call 999 (or 112) and ask for the Coastguard.

items.prompt: Which British sea captain made famous voyages to the Pacific Ocean and mapped New Zealand in the 1760s and 1770s?
items.explain: Cook’s ship on his first voyage was called the Endeavour.

items.prompt: Which explorer’s ship, the Endurance, was crushed by ice in Antarctica, yet he got all his crew home safely?
items.explain: Shackleton sailed a tiny boat 800 miles across stormy seas to get help.

items.prompt: In 1953, Edmund Hillary and Tenzing Norgay were the first to reach the top of which mountain?
items.explain: Everest is the highest mountain in the world, in the Himalayas.

items.prompt: Why was exploring Antarctica so dangerous?

options.text: It is freezing cold and icy
There are lots of hungry lions
options.feedback: No lions! Only penguins and seals.

options.text: It is far too hot and dry
options.feedback: Antarctica is the coldest place on Earth.

items.explain: Explorers had to cope with temperatures far below freezing.

items.prompt: In 1492, which explorer sailed west across the Atlantic and reached the Americas?
items.explain: He was looking for a sea route to Asia, and landed in the Caribbean instead.

items.prompt: What tool did sailors use to find north?
items.explain: A compass needle is a magnet that points north.

items.prompt: Queen Victoria reigned from 1837 to…
items.explain: She reigned for 63 years.

items.prompt: How was a Victorian school different from yours?

options.text: They had computers in every room
options.feedback: No computers! They used slates and chalk.

options.text: There were no teachers at all
options.feedback: There were teachers, and they were very strict.

items.explain: Children sat in rows, chanted their tables and wrote on slates.

items.prompt: What hard job did some poor Victorian children do?

options.feedback: There were no aeroplanes yet.
Space travel came 100 years later.

items.explain: Laws were slowly passed to stop young children working and send them to school.

items.prompt: In 1840 Britain made the world’s first postage stamp. What was it called?
items.explain: It had Queen Victoria’s head on it and cost one penny.

items.prompt: Which new kind of transport spread across Britain in Victorian times?
items.explain: Railways meant people could travel to the seaside for the first time.

items.prompt: In 1851 the Great Exhibition showed off inventions in a huge building made of glass. What was it called?
items.explain: It was like a giant greenhouse in Hyde Park, London.

items.prompt: Who was the first Tudor king, in 1485?
items.explain: Henry VII won the Battle of Bosworth. His son was Henry VIII.

items.prompt: Why is the Tudor rose red AND white?

options.feedback: It joined two families who had been fighting.

options.text: It was painted twice by mistake
options.feedback: It shows two families coming together.

items.explain: Henry VII (Lancaster) married Elizabeth of York, ending the Wars of the Roses.

items.prompt: Henry VIII’s warship sank in 1545 and was raised from the seabed in 1982. What was it called?
items.explain: You can see it in a museum in Portsmouth.

items.prompt: Which Tudor sailor was the first Englishman to sail all the way round the world?
items.explain: Drake sailed in the Golden Hind from 1577 to 1580.

items.prompt: Which famous playwright wrote plays in Tudor times?
items.explain: His plays were performed at the Globe Theatre in London.

items.prompt: Who was the last Tudor monarch?
items.explain: Elizabeth I never married and had no children, so the Tudor line ended with her in 1603.
